analysis.one_liner: Restores broad disability protections under the ADA that courts had narrowed.
analysis.headline: The bill passed the Senate by unanimous consent on September 11 and the House by voice vote on September 17, and President Bush signed it into law on September 25 as Public Law 110-325.
analysis.plain_summary: Supreme Court rulings in 1999 and 2002 had made it much harder for people with disabilities to qualify for protection under the Americans with Disabilities Act, so courts were throwing out discrimination cases from people with diabetes, epilepsy, cancer, and similar conditions. This bill rewrites the definition of disability to cover people whose conditions are controlled by medication or only flare up episodically, and it tells courts to read the law in favor of broad coverage. It passed both chambers with no amendments and became law.
analysis.who_benefits: People with disabilities who were being denied ADA protection after the Supreme Court's Sutton (1999) and Toyota (2002) rulings, which had narrowed coverage to exclude many people Congress originally intended to protect. The bill specifically covers impairments that are episodic or in remission, and it requires that conditions be evaluated without regard to medication, hearing aids, prosthetics, or other mitigating measures [S2] [S6]. People who are discriminated against because they are perceived to have an impairment are also protected, even if the impairment does not actually limit them [S6].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with disabilities facing workplace discrimination

how_it_helps.text: Restores broad scope of protection by rejecting the Supreme Court's Sutton and Toyota standards, which had eliminated protection for many individuals Congress intended to protect [S6].

Expands 'major life activities' to include sleeping, standing, lifting, concentrating, and major bodily functions like immune, neurological, and digestive systems, and covers impairments that are episodic or in remission [S6].

Requires that disability determinations be made without regard to the ameliorative effects of mitigating measures like medication, prosthetics, and hearing aids, so a person whose condition is controlled by treatment is still covered [S2] [S6].

Directs courts to construe the definition of disability in favor of broad coverage, and makes clear that whether someone is disabled should not demand extensive analysis — the focus shifts to whether employers complied with their obligations [S6].
Prohibits employment qualification standards or tests based on uncorrected vision unless they are job-related and consistent with business necessity [S3] [S6].

analysis.who_pays: Employers covered by the ADA — businesses, governments, and other covered entities — bear the cost of broader coverage: more employees qualify for protection, more requests for reasonable accommodation, and greater exposure to discrimination lawsuits. The bill's findings acknowledge the change responds to courts having been too strict, and the EEOC is directed to revise its regulations defining 'substantially limits' to be consistent with the Act [S6].

drawbacks.text: Broader coverage means more accommodation obligations and more discrimination lawsuits for employers, raising compliance costs for businesses of all sizes [S6].

Under the 'regarded as' prong, an individual can claim discrimination without showing any actual limitation on a major life activity, which could open the door to claims based on minor or perceived impairments — though the Act excludes transitory impairments of six months or less and bars reasonable-accommodation claims for people covered only under that prong [S6].

The Act does not change eligibility standards for state workers' compensation or federal disability benefit programs, so it expands employment discrimination protection without touching the benefit systems many disabled workers rely on [S3] [S6].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial: millions of workers with diabetes, epilepsy, cancer, intellectual disabilities, and other conditions regain civil rights protection that courts had stripped away, correcting what Congress found was an interpretation inconsistent with the original 1990 law. The cost falls on employers in the form of compliance obligations and litigation exposure, and the negotiated bill includes several guardrails for them — excluding transitory and minor impairments, barring accommodation claims under the 'regarded as' prong, and leaving benefit programs untouched. On balance this is a genuine expansion of worker protections with acknowledged but limited costs to business.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it by unanimous consent on September 11, the House passed it by voice vote under a fast-track procedure on September 17, and President Bush signed it on September 25, making it Public Law 110-325.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 31, 2008 with 77 cosponsors — 33 Republicans, 42 Democrats, and 1 Independent — showing support across both parties [S7].
The Senate passed the bill without amendment by unanimous consent on September 11, 2008 [S3] [S8].
The House passed the bill by voice vote under suspension of the rules on September 17, 2008, with no amendments [S4] [S8].
President Bush signed the bill on September 25, 2008, and it became Public Law 110-325, effective January 1, 2009 [S5] [S6] [S8].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People with disabilities regained broad civil rights protection, and employers gained clearer, more predictable rules after negotiating the compromise terms.

sides.party_line_note: Support was fully bipartisan: 77 cosponsors split 33 Republicans and 42 Democrats, the Senate passed it by unanimous consent, and the House passed it by voice vote with no recorded opposition [S7] [S3] [S8].

industries.note: Employers face broader coverage, more accommodation requests, and more litigation exposure under the redefined disability standard. But the bill was negotiated with business input and includes employer protections — excluding transitory and minor impairments, barring accommodation claims for people covered only as 'regarded as' disabled, and leaving workers' compensation and benefit eligibility untouched [S3] [S6].

industries.industry: Staffing firms and testing providers using employment tests
industries.note: The bill bars qualification standards and selection criteria based on uncorrected vision unless they are job-related and consistent with business necessity, restricting how employers can screen candidates [S3].
